readerTitle: How a small bookstore competes with a website that sells everything
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 서점, 대학가 카페, 가계부 앱) + 실제 연구 (Raffaelli의 미국 독립서점 연구)
insight: 큰 경쟁자를 이기려면 그가 가장 강한 곳을 피하고, 내가 고른 고객과 무기를 위해 일부러 무언가를 포기한다.
misconception: 작은 가게가 살아남으려면 큰 경쟁자의 가격과 구색을 최대한 따라잡아야 한다.

sources.text: Raffaelli, R. (2020). Reinventing Retail: The Novel Resurgence of Independent Bookstores. Harvard Business School Working Paper.
서점, 카페, 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Raffaelli 연구의 핵심 요소(community, curation, convening, 이른바 '3C')와 그가 Harvard Business School 교수라는 점을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
미국 독립서점이 대형 체인과 온라인 판매 확대로 줄었다가 2009년 무렵부터 다시 늘었다는 흐름은 Raffaelli 연구와 미국서점협회(ABA) 회원 수 자료로 확인하세요. 구체적 수치는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
서점 3,000종, 직원 2명 등 가상 사례의 숫자는 설명용입니다. 계산이 필요한 수치는 없습니다.

cards.title: How a small bookstore competes with a website that sells everything
body: Maya runs a small bookstore on a busy neighborhood street. A customer picks up a new bestseller, checks her phone, and puts the book back. Online, it's cheaper and arrives tomorrow.
Maya can't beat that on price or speed. So where can she win?

image.label: A customer in a small bookstore comparing a book with her phone
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 작은 동네 서점. 손님이 신간 한 권을 들고 휴대폰 화면(가격 비교 화면, 로고 없음)을 보는 장면. 뒤쪽 카운터에 주인이 서 있음. 실제 서점·출판사·온라인몰 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Online is cheaper and faster. What does Maya do?
body: The store carries about 3,000 titles and has two staff. Online sellers carry millions of books at lower prices. Sales are slipping.

options.text: Match online prices on the top bestsellers
options.feedback: This fights on the rival's strongest ground. Maya gives up margin on her best sellers, and the website can always go lower. That's choosing where to play badly.

options.text: Add more of everything: more titles, gifts, toys, a coffee bar
options.feedback: More reasons to visit can help, but spreading thin avoids a real choice. With two staff and a small shop, doing everything means doing nothing especially well.

options.text: Pick a group of local readers and win on what a website can't offer
options.feedback: This is where to play, how to win: choose the customers, then the edge that fits them. The next cards show what that looks like.

cards.eyebrow: Apply · Where to play, how to win
cards.title: Maya picks her ground.
body: **Where to play:** people within a short walk. Maya's street has young families and retirees who read a lot.
**How to win:** things a website can't easily copy. Staff who know the regulars, a hand-picked children's section, Saturday story time, a monthly book club.
The bestseller rack shrinks. The tables of staff picks grow.

image.label: Bookstore floor plan: small bestseller rack, large kids' corner and staff picks
image.brief: 위에서 본 서점 평면도 일러스트. 작게 줄어든 "Bestsellers" 선반, 크게 넓어진 "Kids' corner"와 "Staff picks" 테이블, 의자가 둥글게 놓인 "Story time" 공간. 밝고 단순한 색.

cards.title: Bookstores that came back didn't win on price.
body: In the US, independent bookstores shrank for years as large chains and online sellers grew. Then, around 2009, their numbers began to recover.

Harvard Business School professor Ryan Raffaelli studied that comeback. Stores that grew leaned into **community** (being a local place), **curation** (choosing books for their readers) and **convening** (events that bring people together).
None of the three is about being cheaper.

cards.title: Maya's plan has a price.
body: Every clear choice gives something up. These **trade-offs** are why a giant rival won't simply copy her.
list: **Fewer titles:** some people leave without the book they came for
**Staff time on events:** a higher cost per sale
**No price matching:** bargain hunters go online
**A kids-first layout:** less room for other sections
cards.callout: A website serving millions won't hand-pick books for one street. That's the gap Maya fills.
cards.softwareNote: The same logic protects small software firms: a big platform won't tailor its product to one niche, so the niche is where a small team can win.

cards.title: A clear choice still needs testing.
body: Choosing where to play only works if enough of those customers exist and will pay full price.
Before cutting sections, Maya can track who actually buys, and run a few events to see who comes back. If the families don't show up, she chose the wrong ground. The idea of choosing is still right.

cards.title: A chain coffee shop opens across the street.
body: Your café near a university serves students who study for hours: outlets, quiet tables, refills. The chain is cheaper and faster. An advisor says add a grab-and-go window for commuters.

options.text: Add the window and push speed
options.feedback: It moves you onto the chain's ground, speed and price, where it's stronger. It also adds noise and lines that hurt your study crowd.

options.text: Skip it, and deepen the study offer, like a weekly study pass
options.feedback: You accept the trade-off: fewer quick sales in exchange for loyal, long-staying regulars the chain doesn't want.

options.text: Open the window only before 9 a.m.
options.feedback: Lower risk, since mornings are quiet for students. Still, check whether it pulls staff and attention away from where you've chosen to win.

cards.title: Big banks now offer free budgeting tools.
body: Your small budgeting app charges $5 a month. The banks' free tools work fine for most users. Signups are falling.

options.text: Add every feature the bank tools have
options.feedback: Copying a free rival feature by feature leaves you a smaller version of the same thing, still charging $5.

options.text: Focus on freelancers with uneven income, and build only for them
options.feedback: Where to play, how to win: a narrow group with a need the banks ignore. The trade-off is saying no to users outside it.

options.text: Go free to match the banks
options.feedback: You remove the price gap but also your revenue, and the banks can afford free far longer than you can.

cards.title: Don't fight on the rival's ground. Pick your own, and pay for it.
body: This lesson used two ideas: **where to play, how to win** (choose customers and an edge a big rival can't match) and **trade-offs** (give up what doesn't fit, on purpose).
**Try it today:** finish this sentence: "We serve ___ and win by ___." Then name one thing you'll stop doing because of it.
